books.section: Topic 6.9 Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age

stimulus.text:
Original secondary passage, written for this question from the grounding books:

In the cities of the Gilded Age, immigrants balanced two pulls. Foreign-language newspapers such as the Yiddish-language Jewish Daily Forward and the Italian-language Il Progresso Italo-Americano served whole neighborhoods, and Little Italy and the Jewish Lower East Side of New York grew into worlds of their own, with grocery stores, savings banks, choruses, and political clubs.

At the same time, millions of newcomers, mostly young men, worked part of the year in the United States and spent the rest at home; they were called “birds of passage” for their seasonal coming and going.
stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage, written for this question from Barron’s Premium 2027 Chapter 8 (Topic 6.9), 5 Steps to a 5, 2024, Chapter 18, and Princeton Review, Chapter 10.

stem: According to the passage, what did the foreign-language newspapers and grocery stores show?

options.text: Immigrants kept ties to their home cultures in America
Immigrants refused to work in American factories
options.misconception: Claims a refusal to work the passage never mentions.

options.text: Immigrants were barred from American cities
options.misconception: Claims a ban, but the passage shows immigrants living in cities.

options.text: Immigrants all planned to return home at once
options.misconception: Turns some seasonal migrants into all immigrants leaving at once.

rationales.A: The passage names Yiddish and Italian newspapers and grocery stores selling foods from home, in neighborhoods that grew into worlds of their own. Those are ties to home cultures kept alive inside American cities.
rationales.B: The passage says nothing about immigrants refusing factory work. It describes their neighborhoods, not their jobs.
rationales.C: The passage shows immigrants living in New York neighborhoods with their own stores and clubs. They were not barred from the cities.
rationales.D: Only some newcomers were seasonal migrants. Most stayed and built neighborhoods, so not all planned to return.
rationales.general:
Look at what the newspapers and stores actually did for their readers.
1. Foreign-language papers served whole neighborhoods in their own tongues.
2. Grocery stores sold foods reminiscent of the immigrants' home countries.
3. Little Italy and the Lower East Side grew into worlds of their own.
4. So home cultures lived on inside American cities.
Remember: institutions that serve a language or a food show a culture being kept, not left behind.
